subject: maths
title: Shapes all around us
intro: Shapes are everywhere — a wheel is a circle, a window is a square, a slice of pizza looks like a triangle. Learning the basic shapes helps you notice patterns in the world and is the start of geometry. This lesson introduces the first shapes to know and how to tell them apart.

sections.heading: The first shapes to know
body: Here are three shapes you will see all the time. A **circle** is perfectly round with no corners. A **square** has four straight sides that are all the same length, and four corners. A **triangle** has three straight sides and three corners.
The easiest way to tell shapes apart is to **count the sides and corners**. No corners means a circle. Three corners means a triangle. Four equal sides means a square.

diagram.caption: A circle (no corners), a square (4 sides), and a triangle (3 sides).

sections.heading: A few more shapes
body: There are more shapes to meet. A **rectangle** is like a square but longer on two sides — think of a door or a phone. A **star** has points sticking out. Each shape has its own number of sides and corners, and once you know them you will start spotting them everywhere.
Look around the room right now: how many circles, squares, and rectangles can you find?

diagram.caption: A rectangle (longer on two sides) and a star (with points).

sections.heading: Shapes in the world
body: Shapes aren't just in books — they make up real things. Wheels and clocks are **circles**. Windows and picture frames are often **squares** or **rectangles**. A slice of pizza or a roof can look like a **triangle**.
Noticing shapes in everyday objects is a fun game, and it helps you understand how things are built and how they fit together.

practice.q: How many corners does a triangle have?
practice.explain: A triangle has three straight sides and three corners.

practice.q: Which shape is perfectly round with no corners?
practice.explain: A circle is round all the way around and has no corners at all.

practice.q: A square has how many sides that are the same length?
practice.explain: A square has four straight sides, all the same length, and four corners.

practice.q: A window shaped longer than it is tall is most like which shape?
practice.explain: A rectangle has longer sides on two edges, like a door or a wide window.

practice.q: What is the best way to tell shapes apart?
practice.explain: Counting the sides and corners tells you which shape it is — 3 corners is a triangle, no corners is a circle.

summary: A circle is round with no corners; a square has 4 equal sides; a triangle has 3 sides.
Tell shapes apart by counting their sides and corners.
Shapes are everywhere — wheels are circles, windows are squares or rectangles, roofs can be triangles.
